The lessons are open: text and slides are CC BY 4.0, code is MIT. To teach
them, make your own copy of the repository. One settings file, `event.yml`,
says what kind of run it is, when and where it happens and who teaches it;
the website builds from it, with your dates, schedule and links. The idea is
the one of The Carpentries'
[workshop template](https://github.com/carpentries/workshop-template): one
repository per run, one file to fill in.

## Choose a format

Every format has all the lessons, slides and cheat sheets. They differ in the
schedule and in what the home page and menus show.

- **Course**, `format: course-7week`: seven weeks, with two 80-minute
  lectures and a 110-minute lab a week. The site also shows the 7-week
  schedule, the syllabus, and the assessment pages in the menu.
- **Four-day workshop**, `format: workshop-4day`: four days of about six
  teaching hours. The site also shows the core lessons day by day, with time
  for participants' own projects every day, and the dates, place, people and
  links on the home page.
- **Five-day workshop**, `format: workshop-5day`: the same over five days,
  with more lessons and a gentler pace.
- **Self-paced**, `format: self-paced`: no schedule; learners follow the
  [contents](contents.qmd).

Each format's schedule is a file in `schedules/`: `course-7week.yml`,
`workshop-4day.yml` and `workshop-5day.yml` ([Fit the schedule](#fit-the-schedule)).

## Make your copy

1. **Fork the repository**: press *Fork* on
   <https://github.com/khan-lab/cbio7501-f26>, and give your copy a name for
   your run, for example `ros-2027-01`.
2. **Get it on your computer.** You need Git and
   [Pixi](pages/00-setup.qmd#install-pixi):

   ```bash
   git clone git@github.com:YOUR-USER/YOUR-REPO.git
   cd YOUR-REPO
   ```

3. **Start from an example.** `event.yml` in the repository holds the
   settings of the CBIO7501 course; `events/` has examples for the two
   workshops. Copy one over it:

   ```bash
   cp events/workshop-4day.yml event.yml
   ```

   For a course, edit `event.yml` as it is; for self-paced lessons, set
   `format: self-paced`.
4. **Fill it in** ([the settings](#the-settings)). Under `website:`, put the
   address of your repository and of your site, which on GitHub Pages is
   `https://YOUR-USER.github.io/YOUR-REPO/`.
5. **Look at the site.** `pixi run preview` builds it and opens it in your
   browser, and rebuilds it as you edit; `pixi run render` builds it into
   `_site/`. Read the build output for warnings about the schedule
   ([Fit the schedule](#fit-the-schedule)).
6. **Publish it.** On GitHub, in your copy: *Settings* → *Pages* → *Build and
   deployment* → *Source*: **GitHub Actions**. GitHub turns workflows off in a
   new fork: open the *Actions* tab and enable them. Then commit and push to
   `main`. The *Website* workflow builds the site and publishes it at your
   address.

## The settings

All in `event.yml`, under `event:`. Leave empty what you do not use: empty
settings are left out of the site.

| Setting | What it changes |
|---------|-----------------|
| `format` | which site is built ([Choose a format](#choose-a-format)) |
| `title`, `code`, `institution`, `term` | the home page heading and the line above it, the slide subtitles and footers, the course schedule and syllabus |
| `meetings` | courses: when the course meets, one line per session, on the home page and the syllabus |
| `start-date` | workshops: the dates on the home page, and the date of each day on the schedule |
| `day` | workshops: when the day starts and ends, when lunch starts and how long it and the breaks last; the schedule's times come from it |
| `venue`, `online`, `instructors`, `helpers`, `contact`, `links` | workshops: the table of details on the home page (registration, shared notes, chat, surveys, code of conduct); courses: the instructors on the syllabus |
| `grading` | courses: the credits and each project's share of the grade ([Grading](#grading)) |
| `cluster` | the optional cluster steps in the lessons ([A cluster](#a-cluster)) |

Under `website:` are your repository and site addresses, and the GitHub link
in the menu bar.

## Fit the schedule

The schedules are built from the files in `schedules/`:

- `modules.yml`: each part of a lesson that is taught in one go, with its
  planned length in minutes.
- One file per format, `course-7week.yml`, `workshop-4day.yml` and
  `workshop-5day.yml`: which modules go in which session or day, in order.

To change a schedule, move module ids in the format's file. A workshop day
also takes `break`, `lunch` and any other text, with its length at the end in
brackets:

```yaml
days:
  - title: "Organize and track"
    blocks:
      - "01-slides"
      - "break"
      - "02-organization"
      - "lunch"
      - "Your own project under Git (30)"
```

The times are computed from `day:` in `event.yml`, so moving one module moves
everything after it. Modules that a workshop leaves out are listed under its
schedule, as self-paced. A course session (`lecture-1`, `lecture-2`, `lab`,
`home`) lists modules the same way. The build warns when a course session
holds more minutes than it has, when a morning runs into lunch or a day past
its end, and when a module id is not in `modules.yml`.

When you have taught a module, note how long it really took and change its
`minutes:` in `modules.yml`: every schedule that uses it follows. That is how
the timings get better with each run.

## A cluster

If your participants have an HPC cluster, describe it in `event.yml`:

```yaml
  cluster:
    enabled: true
    name: "Hilbert"
    login: "login.hpc.example.org"
    scheduler: "slurm"
    docs: "https://hpc.example.org/docs"
```

The lessons then use the cluster's name (lesson 08 suggests running
[Apptainer](pages/08-containers.qmd#apptainer) on it), and
[05 §10](pages/05-pixi.qmd#pixi-on-an-hpc-cluster-optional) (Pixi on a
cluster) and [09 §13](pages/09-snakemake.qmd#extra-running-on-a-slurm-cluster)
(Snakemake on Slurm) show how to log in and where its user guide is. Without
a cluster, those two sections fold into a collapsed note, *Optional: on an
HPC cluster*, and the lessons speak of "your cluster".

The cluster steps are not tested automatically, and the Snakemake profile in
lesson 09 is written for Slurm: try them on your cluster before you teach.

## Grading

For courses. With `grading: enabled: true`, the syllabus, the
[LTEE project](pages/ltee-project.qmd) page and the two assessment pages show
each project's share of the grade, from `ltee-project:` and `capstone:`
(percent), and the syllabus shows `credits:`. The rest of the grade, the
deadlines and the policies belong in your official syllabus. Workshops leave
grading off: the two projects are then described without grades.

## Checklists

### Weeks before

- Book a room with power for every laptop, a projector, and Wi-Fi that
  reaches conda-forge, bioconda, GitHub, figshare and NCBI.
- Find helpers: people who know the tools and can unblock a participant
  while you teach. They do not need to know the lessons by heart.
- If participants will use a cluster, fill in `cluster:` and check they have
  accounts.
- Publish your site and send its address with the registration.

### One to two weeks before

- Send the [setup](pages/00-setup.qmd), including
  [step 8](pages/00-setup.qmd#fill-the-cache-before-class), which downloads
  the course software at home: about 2 GB, too much for a room of laptops on
  one Wi-Fi.
- Ask everyone to run the [setup check](pages/00-setup.qmd#setup-check), and
  offer an hour to help those who get stuck. Windows users need WSL2, which
  needs administrator rights once; [GitHub Codespaces](pages/00-setup.qmd#the-fallback-github-codespaces)
  is the fallback.
- Participants need a GitHub account with an SSH key
  ([setup, step 5](pages/00-setup.qmd#git-and-github)) from lesson 04 on.
- Run the tests in your copy: *Actions* → *Tutorials* → *Run workflow*. It
  runs every lesson in a fresh folder on Linux and macOS, with today's
  packages.
- Try what is not tested automatically: the steps on GitHub's web pages
  (pull requests, Pages, Codespaces), the release in
  [lesson 12](pages/12-putting-it-together.qmd) on the Zenodo sandbox, and
  the cluster steps.

### During

- Share one notes document (`links: notes:`) for links, questions and the
  commands you type.
- Type the commands as you teach, at the participants' pace, rather than
  showing them finished.
- Give everyone two colors of sticky notes: one on the laptop means "done",
  the other "I need help". Helpers go to the second.
- Write down how long each module takes.
- At the end of each day, ask for one thing that worked and one to change.

### After

- Send the survey (`links: post-survey:`).
- Update the minutes in `schedules/modules.yml` with the times you noted, and
  move what did not fit.
- Send fixes for the lessons to the original repository, as an
  [issue or pull request](https://github.com/khan-lab/cbio7501-f26/issues).
- Leave the site up: participants come back to it, and what the workshop
  left out is self-paced.

## Keep your copy up to date

Fixes to the lessons arrive in the original repository. To bring them into
your copy, press *Sync fork* on its GitHub page. Changes you keep to
`event.yml` and `schedules/` are easy to carry along: if a sync conflicts
there, keep your version. To change the lessons themselves, see the
[contributor guide](https://github.com/khan-lab/cbio7501-f26/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md):
every command in a lesson is also a test.

## Credit

Keep the license files and the [Sources and credits](pages/credits.qmd) page
in your copy. When you teach from it, credit these lessons and the sources
they adapt, and say what you changed: that is what CC BY 4.0 asks.
